title: How was Pompeii frozen in time?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: In one day, a volcano froze this city for almost 1,700 years.
beats.say: In one day, a volcano froze this city for almost seventeen hundred years.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: How was Pompeii frozen in time?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Today, Pompeii is a ruin near Naples, and millions of tourists walk its streets every year.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: What was it like in AD 79?
beats.say: What was it like in A D seventy-nine?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: A busy Roman town of more than ten thousand people, with bakeries, bars, baths and a theatre.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Above it stood Mount Vesuvius, green with vineyards. It had been quiet for centuries, so nobody feared it.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: So what happened?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: One afternoon, the mountain exploded. A column of ash and stone shot thirty-three kilometres into the sky.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: For about eighteen hours, pumice rained down on Pompeii. Roofs caved in, and many people fled.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Nearby, at Stabiae, people ran with pillows tied to their heads against the falling stones.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And the ones who stayed?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Early the next morning, a glowing avalanche of hot gas and ash raced down the mountain, and killed everyone still in the city.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Did anyone see it happen?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, sailed in to help and died on the shore.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Pliny's letters about it are the only eyewitness account that survives.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: How was the city found again?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Up to six metres of ash buried it, and it was forgotten. Digging began in 1748.
beats.say: Up to six metres of ash buried it, and it was forgotten. Digging began in seventeen forty-eight.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Diggers found hollows in the hard ash, shaped like the people who died there. In 1863, Giuseppe Fiorelli filled them with plaster, and the victims reappeared.
beats.say: Diggers found hollows in the hard ash, shaped like the people who died there. In eighteen sixty-three, Giuseppe Fiorelli filled them with plaster, and the victims reappeared.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: What else survived?

cameo.caption: Cave canem: beware of the dog

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Wall paintings, mosaics, loaves of bread left in an oven, and graffiti everywhere: election slogans, love notes and jokes.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: Has it all been dug up?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: No. About a third of the city is still buried, and new rooms and paintings turn up almost every year.

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: Like the video and follow History Sketches for the next episode: Rome at its largest, under Trajan.

beats.speaker: q
beats.text: And tell us in the comments: would you have run, or stayed?

beats.speaker: a
beats.text: And for the people of Pompeii, it all began as an ordinary day.
